name: CRETI: Proptech Funding Data and AI Research for Real Estate
title: CRETI: Proptech Funding Data and AI Research for Real Estate
answer: The Center for Real Estate Technology & Innovation publishes proptech funding research and case studies. Its most useful finding for AI watchers is that more than half of the 70 companies in its 2026 proptech cohort use AI in some form, spanning robotics, document intelligence, underwriting, property operations, mortgage workflows, estimating, brokerage and infrastructure monitoring, with Construction & Development taking roughly $24.3 million of the $43.0 million disclosed.

sections.body: CRETI, the Center for Real Estate Technology & Innovation, publishes research on real estate technology from its site at creti.org. The material read spans monthly and quarterly investment reports, a 2026 venture capital outlook based on a survey of 145 investors, analyses of the 2026 proptech startup cohort and early-stage funding, a study of AI and retail real estate, a survey of multifamily property managers, and case studies of individual companies including Propera and Rely. The pages carry no single publication date beyond the periods they cover, which run through 2025 and into 2026.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The core of the site is funding data. CRETI reports that venture capital investment in proptech totalled $4.2 billion across 126 deals in the third quarter of 2025, with the ten largest rounds accounting for nearly two-thirds of that total. Its October 2025 report counts 41 proptech and adjacent companies raising a combined $2.9 billion at a $5.2 million median round. On the startup side, CRETI's analysis of the 2026 cohort finds that of 70 companies, only 24 are classified as Core PropTech, 36 as Adjacent PropTech and 10 as Tech-Enabled Real Estate, and that more than half use AI in some form, including robotics, document intelligence, underwriting, property operations, mortgage workflows, estimating, brokerage and infrastructure monitoring. Construction & Development is the largest category, with 25 companies and roughly $24.3 million of the $43.0 million disclosed. A separate study of early-stage rounds finds 26 U.S. companies raising between $500,000 and $2 million in the first half of 2026, with Y Combinator backing seven of them. CRETI also publishes evidence-led analyses, including one concluding there is no consistent evidence that AI is driving changes in retail store size or rent, and a survey of 325 multifamily property managers finding that 60 percent encounter financial discrepancies monthly.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: CRETI reports $4.2 billion invested across 126 proptech deals in the third quarter of 2025, and $2.9 billion across 41 companies in October 2025 at a $5.2 million median round. In its 2026 cohort of 70 companies, 25 focus on Construction & Development, attracting about $24.3 million of the $43.0 million disclosed, with a median disclosed round of roughly $500,000. Its survey of 145 venture capital investors found 46.15 percent said 2025 performed as expected and 37.50 percent cited capital availability as the dominant challenge. Its multifamily survey of 325 property managers found 60 percent encounter financial discrepancies monthly, and it estimates a $50 annual undercharge per unit costs a 500-unit portfolio $25,000.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: For anyone following AI in real estate, CRETI is a source of primary funding evidence rather than commentary. Its cohort analysis quantifies how much of the current startup wave is AI-based and where that capital is going, notably construction and development. Its case studies show concrete applications, such as Propera generating after-repair values and cash offer ranges in under a minute, and Rely automating audits of leases, rent rolls and compliance documents. Its sceptical retail analysis is equally useful, arguing that AI acts as a performance amplifier rather than a pricing mechanism, which gives readers a counterweight to vendor claims.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Real Estate

sections.body: The site is a research publisher with a clear investment focus, so its output is weighted toward funding rounds and market structure rather than technical evaluation or independent benchmarking of AI systems. Several reports rest on CRETI's own datasets and surveys, whose methodologies are not set out in the pages read. Coverage is uneven by period, with some months and quarters reported in detail and others absent, and the case studies read as profiles of selected companies rather than comparative assessments.
